title: What do the odd numbers build?
hook: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 looks like a random pile. Add one more and watch what it builds.

knows: that 4 x 4 = 16 is a square number
doesNotKnow: the formula for the sum of the first n odd numbers

misconception: A running sum of odd numbers is an irregular total you have to grind out term by term; there is no shape or pattern behind it.
objective: The learner can explain, with the L-shaped picture, why the first n odd numbers always add up to n x n: each odd number is exactly the L that grows an n-by-n square into the next square.

claims.text: The sum of the first n odd numbers, 1 + 3 + ... + (2n - 1), equals n x n.
claims.source: Induction: n^2 + (2n + 1) = (n + 1)^2. Classical result (Nicomachus, Introduction to Arithmetic, c. 100 CE); see Nelsen, Proofs Without Words (MAA, 1993), p. 71.

claims.text: Wrapping an n-by-n square of dots with one row and one column (sharing a corner) adds 2n + 1 dots, which is the next odd number, and makes an (n + 1)-by-(n + 1) square.
claims.source: The L-shaped gnomon has n + n + 1 = 2n + 1 dots. Nelsen, Proofs Without Words (MAA, 1993), p. 71.

claims.text: 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + 19 (the first ten odd numbers) equals 100, and the first 100 odd numbers add up to 10,000.
claims.source: Apply c1 with n = 10 and n = 100: 10 x 10 = 100, 100 x 100 = 10,000. Direct addition confirms the n = 10 case.

claims.text: Wrapping a 3 x 3 square takes 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 dots, and 7 is the next odd number. Wrapping a 9 x 9 square takes 9 + 9 + 1 = 19 dots and makes 10 x 10.
claims.source: Instances of c2 with n = 3 (3 + 3 + 1 = 7) and n = 9 (9 + 9 + 1 = 19, the tenth odd number). v2 rewords the 9 x 9 sentence as wrapping (fact-check 2026-10-12 fix 1); the stage caption shows the same split for every L: '(n-1) + (n-1) + 1 (corner)'.

claims.text: The first 15 odd numbers, 1 + 3 + ... + 29, add up to 225.
claims.source: Recall question. Apply c1 with n = 15: 15 x 15 = 225; the 15th odd number is 2 x 15 - 1 = 29.

recall.question: Without adding them one by one: what is 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + 29 (the first 15 odd numbers)?
recall.why: Each odd number is the L that grows a square by one: 15 odd numbers build a 15 x 15 square, which is 225.
